source: Cambodia National IPM Program (MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension), in cooperation with FAO — "Cabbage Integrated Pest Management: An Ecological Guide" (adapted from J.W. Ketelaar & A.L.M. Abubakar), August 2008, 266 pages, Chapter 1 section 1.4
text:
Cabbage's scientific name is given as Brassica oleracea var. capitata, a member of the cruciferous (mustard) family, named for its cross-shaped, four-petaled flowers. The source states cabbage is believed to have originated near Mediterranean and Asia Minor coastal regions, with cultivation dating back to at least the Roman Empire, and notes that wild ancestral forms of the cabbage plant can still be found today growing on coastal cliffs in parts of Europe (England, France, and other European coasts).

The source recounts a specific history of cabbage's spread into South/Southeast Asian highland growing areas: Sir William Baker, a Governor of Ceylon (Sri Lanka), oversaw the establishment of the hill station at Nuwara Eliya, where cabbage and other cool-climate vegetables grew well; from there, cabbage seed spread to other areas such as Colombo and Trincomalee. The crop's further introduction into hill/highland growing areas in the wider region -- including the Nilgiri Hills and the Cameron Highlands -- is attributed to this Sri Lankan cool-highland cultivation, citing historical references (Backer 1996; Senewiratne and Appadurai 1966; Macmillan 1936).

Botanically, cabbage belongs to Brassica oleracea. The source describes the plant's characteristic head-forming growth habit: outer leaves are more open and spread out, while inner leaves fold and layer tightly together, forming the dense round head as the plant matures -- the inner leaves keep developing and are compressed under the pressure of the surrounding outer canopy, producing the compact head shape typical of the crop. Modern commercial varieties have been developed through crossbreeding/hybridization to produce hybrid varieties suited to different climates and growing conditions.
caveat: This source is a 266-page FAO/MAFF IPM manual for cabbage (cabbage Source D); this file covers only section 1.4 (page 4 of the source's own pagination). The three cited historical reference names (Backer 1996; Senewiratne and Appadurai 1966; Macmillan 1936) were legible but their exact original spelling could not be independently verified against a bibliography, since the source does not include one on this page.
